pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Solids, Liquids & Gases

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'States of matter'):** Pupils should be taught to "compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases." Non-statutory guidance: "develop simple descriptions of the states of matter (solids hold their shape; liquids form a pool not a pile; gases escape from an unsealed container)" and group/classify a variety of materials.

- **Standards — US (NGSS, honest gap):** NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to classifying the three states; the nearest is 2-PS1-1 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]', grade 2) and DCI PS1.A. State classification as a distinct topic is UK-led; the US treats it through observable-properties classification and later particle ideas (MS-PS1).

- **Operational details:** Move from naming to systematic classification by BEHAVIOUR, using three reliable tests: does it keep its own shape (solid), does it take the shape of its container and form a level surface (liquid), does it spread out to fill all the available space (gas)? Apply the tests to eight-plus everyday materials and, crucially, work the tricky cases that break naive rules: sand and other powders (they pour like a liquid but each grain is a solid that keeps its shape — a solid); steam (a gas, but the visible white cloud is actually tiny condensed water droplets, not the vapour itself); gels, foams, honey. Make the invisible-gas point concrete (air fills a bag; bubbles are gas). Keep it observational — do not yet require the particle model — but the behaviour patterns lay its groundwork.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (concrete→classifying). The child can define each state by its behaviour, sort eight or more everyday materials with a behaviour justification, and correctly resolve at least one tricky case (sand is a solid; steam is a gas) rather than sorting by appearance.
bestPractices: Classify by three behaviour tests (keeps shape / takes container shape / fills the space), not by look or feel alone.
Deliberately teach the tricky cases — sand and powders (pour but are solids), steam (gas vs visible droplets) — because they expose and correct the naive rules.
Make gases tangible: trap air in a bag, watch bubbles, feel a puff, so 'gas is real stuff' is evidenced, not asserted.
Test a liquid in different-shaped containers to show it takes the container's shape while keeping the same amount — the defining liquid behaviour.
Use consistent sorting criteria and record reasons, extending the classify-from-evidence skill from earlier grouping work.
Keep explanations observational at KS2; treat any particle talk as a light bridge, not a requirement (per DfE guidance).
keyRepresentations: A three-behaviour test chart (keeps shape / fills container / fills all space)
A same-liquid-in-different-containers demonstration (shape changes, amount stays)
Tricky-case cards: sand/powder (pours but solid), steam (gas vs droplets), honey, foam
A trapped-air bag / bubble demo making a gas observable
An eight-plus material sort with behaviour justifications
commonMisconceptions: Sorting by appearance — anything that pours (sand, salt, powder) is called a liquid, missing that each grain is a solid.
Gases are not matter / are weightless / are 'nothing', because they are usually invisible ('seeing is believing').
Believing the visible white cloud of 'steam' IS the water vapour, rather than tiny condensed droplets (the true vapour is invisible).
Thinking a liquid changes amount when it changes container shape (confusing shape with quantity).
Assuming very thick liquids (honey, gel) or very light solids (foam) can't be classified, or classifying them by feel rather than behaviour.

learn.summary: For children aged 8–9 classifying materials as solids, liquids or gases. The core objective is to sort by BEHAVIOUR rather than appearance, using three reliable tests: does it keep its own shape (solid), does it take the shape of its container and form a level surface (liquid), does it spread out to fill all available space (gas)? Learners apply these tests to eight or more everyday materials and work the tricky cases that break naive rules: sand and powders (they pour but each grain is a solid that keeps its shape), steam (a gas, but the visible white cloud is condensed water droplets, not the invisible vapour), plus gels, foams and honey. Gases are made observable and tangible so 'gas is real stuff' is evidenced, not asserted. Explanations stay observational; the particle model is a light bridge, not a requirement at this stage.

activities.title: Test the state bench: pour, seal, observe, sort
feedback: If a learner calls sand a liquid because it pours, direct attention to one grain: is that single grain hard with a fixed shape, or runny? Contrast the pouring PILE with the fixed GRAIN.
If a learner thinks water becomes 'less' or 'more' when it changes container shape, line up the same amount poured back and forth: the shape changes, the quantity does not.
If a learner sorts by feel or looks, ask them to say which of the three behaviour tests they actually observed before placing the item.
activities.rationale: Classification by behaviour is built by acting on substances and watching them respond; pouring into varied containers and observing makes the defining liquid behaviour (takes shape, keeps amount) and the sand case concrete. A hands-on bench or an interactive lets learners generate the evidence rather than being told the conclusion. A physical tray of real substances and jars serves the same purpose; a screen bench is one way to allow safe, repeatable manipulation (e.g. tilt/seal the jar, zoom to show solid grains), and a simulation is a safe way to show a gas visibly filling a container — a pre-prepared sealed demonstration works too.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'States of matter' statutory: 'compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases'; non-statutory 'solids hold their shape; liquids form a pool not a pile; gases escape from an unsealed container'.

Elementary misconceptions: sorting by appearance (powders as liquids), gas as non-matter, and the visible white 'steam' being mistaken for the water vapour rather than condensed droplets; conceptual change needs hands-on repeated observation.
learnerActions: Take each mystery substance and pour or place it into jars of different shapes; observe and record what happens.

Note which items keep the same shape in every jar (e.g. a wooden block) and which pool flat and take each jar's shape (e.g. water); then observe a gas swelling to fill a whole sealed jar (shown via a simulation/animation or a pre-prepared safe sealed demonstration — not a real coloured gas released in class), and see in the simulation that an open container would let the gas escape.
For the water, pour the same amount into several differently-shaped containers; confirm the shape changes while the amount stays the same.
Drop each tested item into a solid / liquid / gas bin and attach a short behaviour tag stating WHY (e.g. 'keeps its own shape', 'takes the jar's shape and lies flat', 'fills the whole space').

Test sand deliberately: pour it (it pours a bit like a liquid, but it heaps into a sloping pile instead of lying flat like water), then look closely at a single grain — note that each grain is hard and keeps its own shape, so classify sand as a solid because the GRAINS keep shape even though the pile pours.
activities.intendedInsight: A material's state is decided by how the material itself behaves (does it keep its own shape, take a container's shape, or fill all the space), not by whether it pours or how it looks. Sand pours but is a solid because each grain keeps its shape.

activities.title: Steam vs the white cloud
feedback: If a learner points to the white cloud as 'the gas', point out the clear gap just above the spout — that gap is the invisible vapour; the cloud further up is where it cooled into droplets.
If a learner says the cold plate 'made' new water, explain the plate cooled the vapour so it turned back into liquid droplets you can now see.
Connect to breath on a cold day: the visible mist is also tiny droplets, not the gas.
activities.rationale: The kettle cloud is a canonical tricky case that exposes the 'seeing is believing' misconception about gases. A predict-then-observe sequence forces the belief into the open before the demonstration corrects it. This activity needs a real (adult-handled) or faithfully simulated demonstration because the resolution comes from seeing the clear gap and the condensing droplets.
sourceClaims: Elementary misconceptions: sorting by appearance (powders as liquids), gas as non-matter, and the visible white 'steam' being mistaken for the water vapour rather than condensed droplets; conceptual change needs hands-on repeated observation.
learnerActions: With an adult handling the kettle safely, watch a boiling kettle and look for the small CLEAR gap right at the spout before the white cloud begins.
Before any reveal, predict which part is the actual gas (the real steam) and explain why.
Watch an adult hold a cold plate or spoon in the plume: observe droplets of liquid water forming on it.
State in your own words: the invisible part near the spout is the gas (water vapour); the white cloud higher up is tiny liquid droplets that have cooled and condensed.
activities.intendedInsight: True water vapour (steam) is an invisible gas; the visible white cloud above a kettle is tiny condensed liquid droplets, not the gas itself. 'I can see it, so that's the gas' is the belief to correct.

activities.title: Gas is real stuff
feedback: If a learner says a sealed 'empty' bottle contains nothing, have them squeeze it and feel the trapped air push back.

If a learner says gas weighs nothing, note the invisibility is why it feels that way; weighing a ball pumped up hard and then the same ball when soft, on a sensitive balance, can provide counter-evidence (a balloon blown up by mouth usually shows no measurable difference).
activities.rationale: Because gases are usually invisible, learners often treat them as 'nothing' or weightless. Making gas tangible through trapped air and bubbles provides direct evidence that gas is matter. Note: claims about the exact mass of air (e.g. a specific grams-per-litre figure) come from a source not marked verified and are not asserted here as a precise value.
sourceClaims: Elementary misconceptions: sorting by appearance (powders as liquids), gas as non-matter, and the visible white 'steam' being mistaken for the water vapour rather than condensed droplets; conceptual change needs hands-on repeated observation.
learnerActions: Trap air by sealing a bag or squeezing a capped bottle; feel the resistance and note the gas takes up space.
Blow bubbles or feel a puff of air on your hand to sense that the invisible gas is really there.

Compare a ball pumped up hard (e.g. a football inflated with a pump) with the same ball when soft. If a sensitive balance is available, weigh it both ways: the hard-pumped ball should weigh slightly more because extra air has been squeezed in. Discuss whether the gas has mass. (A balloon blown up by mouth is not a good test: the air inside is barely squeezed, so a classroom balance will show little or no difference.)
Answer: can you see the air in this room? Is it still a gas even though it's invisible?
activities.intendedInsight: Gases are real matter: they take up space and have mass, even though they are usually invisible. An 'empty' sealed bottle is actually full of air.

activities.title: Classify and check: the eight-plus material sort
feedback: If a learner is stuck on honey because it is 'in between', ask whether it keeps its own shape or slowly takes the jar's shape and forms a level surface over time (liquid behaviour).
If a learner classifies foam by how light it feels, redirect to the behaviour test: does it keep its own shape?
A recognition-only sort can show the final answer; ask the learner to state the behavioural evidence as well, so you can check the reasoning and not just the conclusion.
activities.rationale: Consolidating classification across many materials, including borderline cases, extends the classify-from-evidence skill and tests whether behaviour reasoning has replaced appearance reasoning. Sorting/matching tasks check the conclusion; pairing each choice with a stated behaviour reason keeps the focus on reasoning. This can be done with physical materials, picture cards, or an interactive sort.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'States of matter' statutory: 'compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases'; non-statutory 'solids hold their shape; liquids form a pool not a pile; gases escape from an unsealed container'.
learnerActions: Sort at least eight everyday materials into solid, liquid or gas, writing the behaviour reason for each.

Include genuinely tricky items — honey, jelly/gel, toothpaste, a solid foam such as a sponge — and decide each by behaviour rather than by how thick or light it feels; if an item shows both solid-like and liquid-like behaviour (e.g. toothpaste or shaving foam), record that it is a tricky mixture and describe what it does.
For each item answer 'which behaviour proves it?' by matching it to one of the three tests.
Explain aloud why sand is a solid and why the kettle cloud is not the gas.
activities.intendedInsight: Consistent behaviour-based criteria help classify awkward materials: very thick liquids (honey) and very light solids (solid foams such as a sponge or polystyrene) are judged by whether they keep their own shape, take a container's shape, or fill the space. Some materials, such as shaving foam, toothpaste or jelly, are mixtures that show some solid-like and some liquid-like behaviour, so it is fine to say they do not fit neatly.

constraints: Keep explanations observational at this age; do not require the particle model. Behaviour patterns lay its groundwork but particle talk should be a light bridge only (per DfE non-statutory guidance).
Any activity involving a boiling kettle or hot steam must be adult-handled; children observe only.
When showing a gas visibly filling a container, use a simulation/animation or an already-safe sealed gas; do not release coloured or hazardous gases around children.

A tap-to-reveal chart or annotated image can consolidate the three tests and label examples, but being fixed it cannot let the learner pour, seal or observe behaviour; use it as a scaffold alongside, not instead of, investigation of the tricky cases.

Quiz/sorting formats assess whether the learner reaches the right classification but do not by themselves elicit the behavioural evidence; pair them with a 'which behaviour proves it?' step and use them to check, not replace, hands-on observation.

Do not assert a precise mass-per-litre value for air to learners; the supporting source for that figure is not marked verified. The qualitative point (gas has mass and takes up space) is well supported by the tangible demonstrations.
Sand being a solid depends on recognising each grain keeps its shape; ensure learners look at an individual grain, not just the pouring pile.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claim that '~1 litre of air ≈ 1 g' comes from a source marked verified:false. It is not stated as a precise fact in the learner activities; only the qualitative 'gas has mass and takes up space' is used. Reviewers should confirm any numeric figure before presenting it.

The original row framed a screen bench as uniquely able to deliver the evidence and claimed 3D and dialogue formats add little; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to format-neutral guidance (real materials, cards, or interactives can all work, each with trade-offs).

The NGSS gap noted in pedagogy (no dedicated US performance expectation for three-state classification; nearest is 2-PS1-1 / PS1.A, with particle ideas at MS-PS1) is an honest curriculum-coverage limitation, retained here for reviewer awareness.

The coloured-gas-filling example was re-scoped to a simulation/animation or a pre-prepared safe sealed demonstration because releasing a real coloured gas around young children is unsafe; the 'escapes an open container' contrast is framed as the simulated illustration, since a sealed demo cannot show escape. The conceptual point (a gas expands to fill its container) is unchanged.

assess.poeTask: With the teacher handling a kettle safely, boil it and point out the small CLEAR gap right at the spout before the white cloud begins. Ask the child to PREDICT which part is the actual gas (the steam) and WHY, before revealing. Most point at the white cloud. Then hold a cold plate in the plume: droplets form, showing the 'gas' turning back to liquid water. The pre-reveal reasoning is diagnostic — 'I can see it so that's the gas' exposes the belief that gases are visible.
probeDeeper: One grain of sand under a magnifier — is that grain hard, or runny?
Can you see the air in this room? Is it still a gas even though it's invisible?
Is jelly a solid or a liquid? What about honey, or toothpaste?
Exactly where is the steam above the kettle — the clear bit near the spout, or the cloudy bit higher up?
assess.correctAnswer: Sand is a SOLID: it's made of many tiny solid grains, each keeping its shape; the pile pours only because the grains slide over one another. The white cloud above a kettle is NOT the gas — true steam (water vapour) is invisible; the white cloud is tiny liquid droplets that have condensed as the vapour cooled.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Pours means liquid' — classifies powders and grains as liquids because they flow.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Examine one grain under a magnifier — a hard solid with a fixed shape; contrast the pouring PILE with the fixed GRAIN.
errorPatterns.distractor: Sand is a liquid because it pours and takes the shape of the bucket.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls sand, sugar or salt a liquid.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The visible white cloud is the gas' — mistakes condensed droplets for the vapour; believes you can see a gas.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Note the clear gap just above the spout (that's the invisible vapour); the white cloud further up is where it has cooled into tiny liquid droplets.
errorPatterns.distractor: The white cloud above the kettle is the gas — that's what steam looks like.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points at the kettle plume (or breath on a cold day) as 'the gas'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gas is not matter — an 'empty' bottle has nothing in it; a gas weighs nothing and isn't a real substance.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fan the air, squeeze a sealed bottle, weigh an inflated vs deflated ball — gases are real matter that take up space and have mass.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a gas isn't a material, or that a sealed 'empty' bottle contains nothing.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by a single surface behaviour (pours = liquid, visible = gas); gets the tricky cases wrong; denies gases are matter.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by what the material IS, resolving the tricky cases — sand is solid grains, the kettle cloud is condensed droplets not the invisible gas — and treats gases as real matter.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts clear-cut solids, liquids and gases correctly and defines them by behaviour, but mishandles the tricky cases (sand, steam) using surface appearance.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Sand pours out of a bucket just like water does. Is sand a solid, a liquid, or something in between — and why?' Then: 'Now think about the white cloud you see above a boiling kettle. Is that cloud the gas (the steam itself), or is it something else?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Sand and the kettle-cloud are the canonical tricky cases. A child reasoning from surface behaviour ('it pours, so liquid'; 'I can see it, so that's the gas') gets both wrong; a child reasoning from what the material IS (solid grains; invisible vapour) gets both right. Tier-2 forces that reasoning into the open.
